families.name: Introductory examples
families.description: Well-known models written afresh for Metascape as short, readable examples.

families.name: Sugarscape
families.description: Epstein and Axtell's Sugarscape as implemented in Ascape, following the chapters of Growing Artificial Societies: foraging, growback, seasons and pollution (II), sex, inheritance and culture (III), and spice and trade (IV).

families.name: Artificial Anasazi
families.description: Agent-based reconstruction of the Kayenta Anasazi of Long House Valley, Arizona, AD 800-1350: households farm maize under the reconstructed climate, and their numbers are compared with the archaeological record of growth and collapse.

families.name: Civil Violence
families.description: Joshua Epstein's civil violence models: rebellion against a central authority (Model I) and violence between two groups with cops as peacekeepers (Model II), with the runs of the paper.

families.name: Norms
families.description: Learning to be thoughtless: a ring of agents who adopt a norm from their neighbors and adapt how many neighbors they consult.

families.name: Retirement
families.description: Coordination in transient social networks: rational, random and imitating agents decide when to retire.

families.name: Emergence of Classes
families.description: A multi-agent bargaining model in which conventions about fair shares, and between tagged groups unequal shares, emerge from local encounters.

families.name: Emergence of Firms
families.description: Employees choose their effort and their firm under local increasing returns; firms form and a skewed distribution of firm sizes emerges.

families.name: Demographic Prisoner's Dilemma
families.description: Joshua Epstein's demographic Prisoner's Dilemma: fixed-strategy players move, play their neighbors, reproduce when rich and die when broke, and zones of cooperation emerge.

families.name: Spatial Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (GA)
families.description: Players on a lattice evolve memory-based strategies for the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma with mutation and crossover, choosing partners at random, by genetic similarity or by an evolved preference.

families.name: Diffusion
families.description: Diffusion in social networks: cells adopt a behavior by its inherent payoff and how many neighbors have adopted it, with random error. Two, three and six actions.

families.name: Conway's Life
families.description: John Conway's cellular automaton in three Ascape forms: the full model, a small-world neighborhood variant and a condensed version.

families.name: Busy Beavers (bb)
families.description: Beavers search for small Turing machines that write the most ones, using a fixed rule, random rules or genetic algorithms.

families.name: Coordination Game (Ascape manual tutorial)
families.description: The tutorial of the Ascape manual: a coordination game on a lattice, built up in five steps from imitation of neighbors to births, deaths and social networks.

families.name: Simple
families.description: The smallest Ascape example: one agent whose happiness doubles every period and an environment that sometimes breaks it.

families.name: Bionland
families.description: A step-by-step Ascape tutorial: a lattice with randomly placed bions gains movement, three species that chase one another, energy, reproduction, diffusion, statistics and other spaces, up to the full model.

families.name: Boids
families.description: Craig Reynolds' Boids (1987) as implemented in Ascape: flocking in a wrapped plane from prioritized local steering rules, with a red team that only avoids obstacles and a blue team that flocks.

families.name: Traffic
families.description: A simple traffic model demonstrating that simple rules can elicit complex traffic behavior such as rolling backups.

families.name: StupidModel
families.description: Steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 of the StupidModel teaching series: bugs wander a grid, then grow, then live on habitats that produce food.

families.name: Wiki Example
families.description: Individuals of different ages on a city grid seek out others of their own age and settle beside them.

families.name: Heatbugs (AMP)
families.description: Bugs that warm their surroundings and seek a preferred temperature on a heat-diffusing grid.

families.name: Demographic Prisoner's Dilemma (AMP)
families.description: Epstein's spatial Prisoner's Dilemma with births and deaths: strategies spread by reproduction, not imitation.

families.name: Epidemic (AMP)
families.description: Epidemic spread through individuals on a grid, with variants that record contacts, add rats and fleas, or link several cities by migration.

families.name: Markets
families.description: Traders, firms and parcels of shares: a small ask-and-buy market in which firm prices follow the trades.

families.name: SIR (system dynamics)
families.description: The classic susceptible, infected and recovered compartment model as stocks and flows.

families.name: Written as data
families.description: Models defined in the declarative model format, with no model code.

models.name: Game of Life
models.summary: Cells live or die by counting their neighbours; gliders and oscillators emerge from three simple rules.
models.description: John Conway's Game of Life (Martin Gardner, Scientific American, October 1970): a two-dimensional cellular automaton in which a live cell survives with two or three live neighbors and a dead cell comes alive with exactly three. Simple local rules produce oscillators, gliders that travel across the lattice and long-lived chaotic growth, and it is the standard demonstration of emergence in agent-based systems.

models.name: Schelling segregation
models.summary: Residents who want only a few like neighbours still end up in sharply divided neighbourhoods.
models.description: Thomas Schelling's segregation model ('Dynamic Models of Segregation', Journal of Mathematical Sociology, 1971). Residents of two groups live on a grid with some empty sites and move to a random vacancy whenever too small a share of their neighbors is like themselves. Even a mild preference for like neighbors drives strongly segregated neighborhoods that nobody intended.

models.name: Sugarscape
models.summary: Agents roam a landscape of sugar, eat to survive, and a skewed distribution of wealth emerges.
models.description: Joshua Epstein and Robert Axtell's Sugarscape, the basic model of chapter II of 'Growing Artificial Societies' (Brookings Institution Press and MIT Press, 1996). Agents with differing vision, metabolism and initial wealth forage for sugar on a landscape with two peaks. Death thins the population to the landscape's carrying capacity, the survivors are the best-adapted, and wealth ends up very unequally distributed even though the rules are identical for everyone.

models.name: Heatbugs
models.summary: Bugs that like a certain warmth give off heat and huddle into clusters that wander and dissolve.
models.description: The Heatbugs model from the Swarm toolkit (Santa Fe Institute, Minar, Burkhart, Langton and Askenazi, 1996). Bugs radiate heat and try to sit at a preferred temperature, while the heat diffuses and evaporates across a torus. No bug is told to cluster, yet the swarm gathers into warm clumps that drift about as each bug seeks the right temperature, a standard illustration of self-organization from purely local rules.

models.name: Wolf Sheep Predation
models.summary: Wolves eat sheep, sheep eat grass; populations boom and crash in predator-prey cycles.
models.description: Wolf Sheep Predation (Wilensky, 1997, NetLogo Models Library), after the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey equations. Sheep wander a wrapped grid eating grass, which regrows slowly; wolves wander and eat sheep. Animals pay energy to move, die when it runs out, and reproduce at random, splitting their energy with the offspring. The agent-based version shows what the equations cannot: oscillating populations that are driven by space, chance and local extinctions.

models.name: Demographic Prisoner's Dilemma
models.summary: Cooperators and defectors play, breed and die on a lattice; clusters of cooperation can survive.
models.description: Joshua Epstein's Demographic Prisoner's Dilemma (Zones of Cooperation in Demographic Prisoner's Dilemma, Complexity, 1998). Fixed-strategy cooperators and defectors wander a torus, play a Prisoner's Dilemma with each neighbor, die when their wealth is negative or they are old, and reproduce when rich. Because play is local and offspring appear next to their parents, clusters of cooperators can survive and grow even though defection pays better in any single encounter.

models.name: Boids
models.summary: Birds follow three local steering rules, and a flock forms with no leader.
models.description: Craig Reynolds' boids (1987): each bird steers by three local rules, separation from crowding neighbors, alignment with the mean velocity of neighbors in sight, and cohesion toward their center, yet the group flocks without any leader or global plan. The model runs in a wrapped square space with synchronous updating and tracks polarization (the length of the mean unit velocity, near 0 for disorder and 1 for perfect alignment) and the mean distance to the nearest neighbor.

models.name: Epidemic (SIR on a small-world network)
models.summary: An infection spreads over a small-world network of contacts until it burns out.
models.description: A susceptible-infected-recovered epidemic spreading over a Watts-Strogatz small-world network (Watts and Strogatz, Nature, 1998) with the compartmental logic of Kermack and McKendrick (1927). Each susceptible person is infected with probability 1 - (1 - transmission)^n, where n is the number of infected neighbors; infected people recover after a fixed period and are immune, permanently or for a limited time. Updating is synchronous, so results do not depend on the order of agents. A few random shortcuts make the outbreak far faster than on a pure ring.

models.description: Agents repeatedly divide a pie by each demanding a low, medium or high share, and each demands whatever would have paid best against its memory of past opponents. Norms of what to demand emerge from these decentralized encounters and then persist, even though they may have arisen from random events. Two tagged groups with 20% random demands; light agents begin expecting low demands from the dark group, dark agents high demands from the light group.
models.authors: Robert L. Axtell, Joshua M. Epstein and H. Peyton Young

models.name: Emergence of Classes: Figure 9
models.summary: Agents repeatedly divide a pie by each demanding a low, medium or high share, and each demands whatever would have paid best against its memory of past opponents.

models.authors: Robert L. Axtell, Joshua M. Epstein and H. Peyton Young

models.name: Emergence of Classes: Model Peyton

models.name: Coordination Game: Step 1
models.summary: Players on a lattice take random steps and play a coordination game with a random neighbor: matching on red or on blue pays the player.
models.description: Players on a lattice take random steps and play a coordination game with a random neighbor: matching on red or on blue pays the player. After a few plays each player copies the colour of any neighbor who is scoring better.

models.name: Coordination Game: Step 2
models.summary: Step 1 with errors: with a given chance a player picks a colour at random instead of imitating.
models.description: Step 1 with errors: with a given chance a player picks a colour at random instead of imitating. The chart adds the average payoff.

models.name: Coordination Game: Step 3
models.summary: Players remember the colours of their last five partners and switch to the colour with the higher expected payoff against them (a best reply), choosing at…
models.description: Players remember the colours of their last five partners and switch to the colour with the higher expected payoff against them (a best reply), choosing at random on ties or with the given error.

models.name: Coordination Game: Step 4
models.summary: Players no longer change colour.
models.description: Players no longer change colour. A player whose last five plays score exactly the reproduction score has an offspring of the same colour on a free neighboring cell; a player with low score after enough plays dies. The population evolves by selection.

models.name: Coordination Game: Step 5
models.summary: Players play their lattice neighbors but imitate four randomly chosen friends anywhere on the lattice, so that conventions spread through a social network…
models.description: Players play their lattice neighbors but imitate four randomly chosen friends anywhere on the lattice, so that conventions spread through a social network instead of through space.

models.name: Simple
models.summary: The smallest Ascape tutorial model: one agent whose happiness doubles every period up to a ceiling, and any other agents, which each have a one in ten chance…
models.description: The smallest Ascape tutorial model: one agent whose happiness doubles every period up to a ceiling, and any other agents, which each have a one in ten chance per period of resetting that happiness. The lattice is part of the model but stays empty.

models.name: Bionland: Step A
models.summary: A bare 25 x 25 lattice with 100 bions dropped at random positions.
models.description: A bare 25 x 25 lattice with 100 bions dropped at random positions. Nothing moves yet: the first step of the Bionland tutorial.

models.name: Bionland: Step B
models.summary: The bions now take a random walk each period, one step to a random neighboring site when it is free, on light gray tiles.
models.description: The bions now take a random walk each period, one step to a random neighboring site when it is free, on light gray tiles.

models.name: Bionland: Step C
models.summary: Three species of bions (red, orange and blue) share the lattice at a chosen overall density and random-walk on black tiles.
models.description: Three species of bions (red, orange and blue) share the lattice at a chosen overall density and random-walk on black tiles.

models.name: Bionland: Step D
models.summary: Bions can now see up to a vision distance and move away from the nearest bion of the species that preys on them (red from blue, orange from red, blue from…
models.description: Bions can now see up to a vision distance and move away from the nearest bion of the species that preys on them (red from blue, orange from red, blue from orange), as well as walking at random.

models.name: Bionland: Step E
models.summary: Each species leaves a coloured energy on the tile it stands on, and eats the energy of the other two species from its tile; the tile colour mixes the three energies.
models.description: Each species leaves a coloured energy on the tile it stands on, and eats the energy of the other two species from its tile; the tile colour mixes the three energies.

models.name: Bionland: Step F
models.summary: The same model as Step E; only the way it is drawn changes (bions as balls rather than squares).
models.description: The same model as Step E; only the way it is drawn changes (bions as balls rather than squares).

models.name: Bionland: Step G
models.summary: Bions now carry stored energy: they pay for living, gain what they eat, split in two when they hold more than 2 and die when they run out.
models.description: Bions now carry stored energy: they pay for living, gain what they eat, split in two when they hold more than 2 and die when they run out.

models.name: Bionland: Step H
models.summary: Bions now follow gradients of tile energy: toward the energy of the species they eat and away from the energy of the species that eats them.
models.description: Bions now follow gradients of tile energy: toward the energy of the species they eat and away from the energy of the species that eats them. An energy gain parameter sets what energy is worth.

models.name: Bionland: Step I
models.summary: As Step H, with statistics: the chart shows each species' average stored energy.
models.description: As Step H, with statistics: the chart shows each species' average stored energy.

models.name: Bionland: Step J
models.summary: Tile energy now spreads: each tile takes the average of its neighbors every period.
models.description: Tile energy now spreads: each tile takes the average of its neighbors every period. The chart now counts bions.

models.name: Bionland: Step K
models.summary: Diffusion now has a diffusion constant and an evaporation rate.
models.description: Diffusion now has a diffusion constant and an evaporation rate. At the defaults (1 and 0) it is the same as Step J.

models.name: Bionland: Step L
models.summary: The lattice now has a von Neumann neighborhood (four neighbors) instead of Moore (eight), which changes walking, diffusion and how far bions can follow energy.
models.description: The lattice now has a von Neumann neighborhood (four neighbors) instead of Moore (eight), which changes walking, diffusion and how far bions can follow energy.

models.name: Bionland: Step M
models.summary: Back on the Moore lattice, drawn with a ring around each bion that shrinks as its stored energy falls.
models.description: Back on the Moore lattice, drawn with a ring around each bion that shrinks as its stored energy falls.

models.name: Bionland: Step P
models.summary: The lattice becomes a one-dimensional ring of 190 sites at 10% density, shown with pure red, orange and blue tile energies.
models.description: The lattice becomes a one-dimensional ring of 190 sites at 10% density, shown with pure red, orange and blue tile energies.

models.name: Bionland: Step Q
models.summary: Red, orange and blue bions chase and flee each other across a continuous 600 x 600 space: each moves toward its nearest prey and away from its nearest predator…
models.description: Red, orange and blue bions chase and flee each other across a continuous 600 x 600 space: each moves toward its nearest prey and away from its nearest predator within its vision, at its own speed.

models.name: Bionland: Step R
models.summary: Fifteen bions of three species chase and flee each other across a random directed graph of 50 nodes, whose links are occasionally rebuilt.
models.description: Fifteen bions of three species chase and flee each other across a random directed graph of 50 nodes, whose links are occasionally rebuilt.

models.name: Bionland: Step S
models.summary: The species chase of Step R on a small-world graph: a ring of two-way links with a few random extra links.
models.description: The species chase of Step R on a small-world graph: a ring of two-way links with a few random extra links.

models.name: Bionland: Full Model
models.summary: Three species chase each other along a ring of 190 sites, each eating the energy of the species it hunts, leaving its own behind, and splitting or dying with…
models.description: Three species chase each other along a ring of 190 sites, each eating the energy of the species it hunts, leaving its own behind, and splitting or dying with its stored energy.
